In brief

Reuniting with Haines in the DBC, Mulligan tells him that "you missed Dedalus on Hamlet," and Haines responds with an oddly poetic yet dismissive interjection: "— I'm sorry, he said. Shakespeare is the happy huntingground of all minds that have lost their balance." While Joyce’s inclinations towards alliteration and compound words may make this phrase sound original, in fact it is a literary allusion loaded with historical freight. In James Fenimore Cooper’s 1823 novel The Pioneers, Chingachgook, a Mohican Native American and companion to series protagonist Natty Bumpo, refers to an idealized afterlife supposedly common to indigenous cultures across America: “Hawk Eye! my fathers call me to the happy hunting grounds.” Haines's sarcastic allusion manages to suggest that Stephen is racially inferior and that his literary endeavors are no better than the superstitions of American Indians. But the phrase may also be read more positively.

At more length

Cooper had an outsized influence on how white readers came to understand Native societies. Though “happy hunting ground” has no authentic origin in any First Nation religious tradition, it was repeated often in settler literature as pseudo-anthropology—a shorthand for the native idea of the afterlife, flattening the complex and varied traditions of many tribes down to an idiomatic cliché. In effect Haines is dismissing Stephen’s theory through a condescending reference. His judgment is soon amended by Buck Mulligan, who adds: “They drove his wits astray…by visions of hell,” casting the blame on Stephen's Irish catholic roots and his Jesuit training. Both men indulge a patronizing send-up of Stephen’s devotion, with Buck taking aim at his renounced faith in the church and Haines mocking his new one for art and literature.

By dismissing Stephen’s belief in interrogating literary texts for deep hidden meanings as an absurdity on par with primitive superstitions, the Englishman imports the dismissive western view of native spirituality into the British colonial context, repeating a frequently heard association between Native Americans and the Irish. Buck stands impartial in this excursion across cultures, though like Stephen he’s an aesthete and as an Irishman he may appreciate the racist implications better than his English companion does. Perhaps by pivoting to Stephen's Christian upbringing, a subject on which he and Haines agree, he is attempting to position himself neutrally and relieve the tension between the roommates. He does not say what he well might: that the previous night's episode involving a black panther and a revolver shows Haines himself to be suffering from an unbalanced mind.

Like many of the mockeries in Joyce's novel, Haines's insult contains some serious insight and may even lend itself to an affirmative reading. Many people, starting with Delia Bacon in the 1840s, have monomanically scoured Shakespeare's works for evidence that he did not write them. In Scylla and Charbydis Stephen uses his extensive reading of plays, poems, biographies, and criticism to advance a highly selective and tendentious account of the author's sexual unhappiness—which might well be called "an idée fixe," as Haines does. Most serious students of Shakespeare will find his "theory" unbalanced, but it holds deep relevance to the artistic patterning of Ulysses. Joyce mined elements from the great playwright to help erect the structures of his novel, just as he did from the epic poems of Homer and Dante. If the result is transcendent, who can complain that the approach lacks "balance"? Bardolatry has always been a kind of secular faith involving hushed reverence for artistic genius. For Joyce this bardic paradise was not an altar but a hunting ground—lush terrain in which he could roam monomaniacally seeking useful material.

Joyce could have encountered the Happy Hunting Ground in a second literary text, Douglas Madden's 1907 The Diary of Master William Silence. Centered mostly on hunting and other sporting practices in the Elizabethan age, Madden's book is a fictional journal by the eponymous William Silence—a nom de plume, it is implied, for William Shakespeare. In the foreword Madden reflects, “Again; and again; I revisited those happy hunting grounds, and in each succeeding autumn the thoroughly Shakespearian character of the sport.” This passage, if Joyce knew it, might well have suggested to him that Shakespeare too was a literary hunter. Taking an epithet applied to the king of the western canon and attaching it, however mockingly, to Joyce's own autobiographical persona implies a kind of transfer of authorial prestige. The Bard's hunting grounds are quite exclusive, but Joyce too tramps those woods.

Michael F. Chefalo and John Hunter 2026
